title: Large-Load Water Tariff Desk for Utilities
one_liner: An advisory-plus-software desk that gives small water and wastewater utilities the tariffs, effluent valuation and contract terms to negotiate with data centers.
customer: Municipal water and wastewater utilities and councils near data-center clusters (Texas, Arizona, Ohio, Georgia, Wyoming, Nebraska), plus investor-owned utilities preparing rate cases (the 15 largest private water companies invested about $6.8B in 2025). The utility pays.
problem: Step one: states restrict potable and groundwater for data centers. Step two: developers turn to treated effluent and offer take-or-pay deals under NDA. Step three: the small utility on the other side has no large-load rate class, no reclaimed-water price, no drought-curtailment priority and no analysis of downstream users who depend on its return flows. Electric utilities built large-load tariffs 12-24 months ago, and water is next.
solution: A 'Large-Load Water Tariff Toolkit': a cost-of-service model for a new large load, minimum-take and curtailment clauses, effluent valuation (including return-flow obligations), construction cost recovery, and reporting and audit clauses matching Texas and Australian rules. Entry product: a one-page 'your effluent is worth $X per acre-foot' for every discharge-permit plant within 30 miles of a data-center cluster, built from public discharge-monitoring data.
why_now: Texas froze ERCOT approvals on Aug 3, Ohio scrapped its general permit, and the Mississippi River states are drafting a compact. Regulators are asking who funds the extra infrastructure. Developers will sign deals in months, and the utility side has no playbook.
revenue_model: $30-150k fixed-fee engagements for tariff design and effluent valuation, SaaS for the cost-of-service model, and a success fee on an executed contract.
non_obvious_insight: The party with new bargaining power is the small wastewater utility, whose effluent just became an asset, but it is the least-staffed party in the room. Advising the weaker side of a deal is where the money is when the stronger side has all the lawyers.
first_30_days: Map all discharge-permit plants near known data-center campuses using public discharge and permit data. Produce 20 one-pagers. Email utility directors and city managers, and offer a free 45-minute briefing. Aim to close two paid engagements of $30-50k.

title: CRA Ten-Year Update Vault for Vendors
one_liner: An escrow-plus-hosting service that keeps a small vendor's signed security updates, vulnerability intake and orphaned open-source dependencies alive for the EU Cyber Resilience Act's ten-year obligation if the vendor folds or an upstream dies.
customer: Small EU-selling firmware, IoT and software vendors (1-50 staff) with no security team, and the enterprise buyers and OEMs who will demand proof of continuity before they buy from them.
problem: CRA reporting duties started 2026-09-11 and the main obligations bite 2027-12-11, with no size exemption. A solo German software founder on HN (Sept 1, 2026) calls the requirement that security updates stay available for ten years, or the support period if longer, a critical burden, and notes reporting duties continue after support ends. Harmonised standards aren't published yet (core standards due Oct 31, 2026). Open-source upstreams also vanish: MinIO (61.3k stars) was archived on 2026-04-25 with no binaries, and 'no fork has gained traction'.
solution: Three parts. (1) Escrow: a reproducible-build environment, SBOM/VEX and split-custody signing keys held by the vault, released on contractual trigger events (insolvency, abandonment, twelve months without a patch). (2) Continuity hosting: a signed-update endpoint and advisory feed that stays online for ten years, plus a vulnerability-report intake and drafts for the EU single reporting platform. (3) Dependency lifeboat: patch backports and maintained forks of orphaned components that customers depend on (MinIO first). Vendors get a 'continuity certificate' to attach to tenders.
why_now: Reporting obligations are 17 days old as of today, standards are still being written, and small vendors are asking on HN what to do. The EU's own guidance creates open-source 'stewards' who face obligations but are exempt from fines, while manufacturers carry the burden, so the market will look for a commercial steward.
revenue_model: Annual escrow and hosting fee per product (EUR 1.5k-6k), a per-release fee, trigger-event activation fee, and dependency-lifeboat support contracts priced per node.
non_obvious_insight: The CRA turns 'what if you disappear?' from a founder worry into a legal duty, and escrow-style insurance sells to both the vendor and the buyer who fears the vendor's death; the compliance-tooling crowd (scanners, SBOM dashboards) does not cover it. Evidence: Ask HN by a one-person vendor on the ten-year update rule, harmonised standards timing and no size exemption (https://hn.algolia.com/api/v1/items/49520688). The EU says stewards are not subject to administrative fines (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/cra-open-source), with the 11 Sept 2026 and 11 Dec 2027 dates at https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/cyber-resilience-act. Linux Foundation research finds most open-source respondents unfamiliar with the CRA and its deadlines (https://linuxfoundation.org/research/cra-readiness). Greg Kroah-Hartman's explainer says the burden lands on commercial manufacturers (https://www.theregister.com/2025/09/30/cyber_reiliance_act_opinion_column/). Upstream death example: https://github.com/minio/minio.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: write the escrow and trigger-event contract template with an EU tech lawyer, and prototype a reproducible-build capture for one embedded Linux and one Go or Rust project. Days 10-30: post a plain-English 'CRA ten-year problem' guide on HN, the Open Regulatory Compliance working group hub and embedded-vendor communities, and offer 10 founders a free continuity assessment. Sell 3 paid pilot vaults at a founder price of EUR 1k a year. In parallel, publish a MinIO advisory-and-patch feed to test paying demand for the lifeboat.

title: Tariff Forward Curve for Section 232 Lists
one_liner: A probability feed for which HTS codes join the next Section 232 lists, with parametric hedges to follow.
customer: CFOs and sourcing heads at importers with metal-heavy lines and $20M-$1B revenue, and trade counsel. Insurers and MGAs later.
problem: Firms treat tariffs as unpredictable, so they pre-buy a year of inventory or freeze decisions. But Section 232 additions run through a public administrative pipeline of industry petitions and comment periods (the latest request for comments on 2026-08-06). Other actions carry visible dates: polysilicon at 15% with minimum import prices from 2026-12-04, and a robotics and machinery investigation still pending. Nobody publishes odds.
solution: Model each HTS-10's probability and timing of inclusion or rate change using past inclusion rounds (petitioner identity, domestic producer concentration, import share, comment volume). Update as dockets move. Deliver a dashboard, API and Slack alerts. Phase 2 is a parametric cover with an MGA or event-contract venue that pays if a heading's rate rises by a set amount within 12 months, priced off the curve.
why_now: With IEEPA gone, Section 232 is the main channel. The inclusion process is open and docketed, LLMs can read comments at scale, and event-contract and parametric markets have grown.
revenue_model: $1.5-5k a month subscription. Later, commission or spread on hedges.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders call tariffs political noise, but 232 additions follow petitioners who show up months earlier. Even 65% accuracy is worth far more than the fee to a firm deciding whether to pre-buy. Tracking current rates is crowded, but forecasting future inclusion is not.
first_30_days: Scrape BIS inclusion dockets and Federal Register notices. Hand-label the last two rounds. Publish a free weekly 'next 232 list watch' newsletter. Sign five paid pilots from importers with more than $500k of metal-derivative exposure.

title: Human Trust-Anchor Service for Driverless Freight Hubs
one_liner: A neutral crew and signature service at autonomous-truck terminals that replaces the driver's role as freight's witness: pre-trip inspection, condition-of-freight capture, signed digital BOL and inspector liaison, priced per handoff.
customer: Autonomous trucking carriers, the shippers, 3PLs and brokers tendering freight to them, and cargo insurers. The first buyer is a claims-sensitive shipper or a broker like Werner's CIO who says 'we have a gap'.
problem: The driver signs the BOL, counts pieces, notes damage, checks the seal and talks to the inspector. Driverless trucks remove that witness. The CVSA enhanced-inspection clearance lasts 24 hours and requires a trained inspector. PrePass/Kodiak bypass covers 581 sites but is live only in Texas and Louisiana. Paper BOLs delay cash about 60 days and cause six-figure invoice disputes. Hub-to-hub autonomy leaves 'hundreds of dollars' of human transfer cost per handoff. Insurers price AV trucks above human ones purely on the unknown.
solution: A per-departure witness desk at transfer hubs and terminals, staffed by trained ex-drivers and ex-inspectors with capture tools. It runs the pre-trip enhanced-inspection checklist and logs the 24-hour clearance. It captures condition of freight (piece count, seal number, photos, weight, temperature, damage detection) and issues a neutral third-party-signed eBOL that shipper, carrier and insurer accept. It also acts as the roadside and first-responder liaison, and packages claims evidence.
why_now: Aurora exits 2026 with about 200 driverless trucks and targets 30,000 by 2030. Gatik reports 85k driverless orders. California's driverless-truck rules took effect Apr 28, 2026 and the Teamsters sued on Aug 5. NHTSA sent a first-responder letter on Jul 8, 2026. Insurers expect AV truck pricing to fall 15-25% a year, so evidence of loads and conditions moves pricing.
revenue_model: $35-$90 per handoff or departure, well under the current human transfer cost. $4k-$8k/mo per hub as a base fee. Insurer-paid discounts and data license. Claims-evidence packages at $150-$400 per incident.
non_obvious_insight: Driverless trucking is sold as removing labor, but what it actually removes is a witness, and freight claims, inspections and insurance pricing all ran on that witness. Whoever re-supplies trusted witness capacity at transfer hubs becomes a required, neutral node. Because the same crew and signature service serve every AV carrier, no competing carrier will build it.
first_30_days: Pick one Texas corridor and one terminal. Recruit 2-3 ex-inspectors or ex-drivers. Offer a shipper's claims team or a broker a free pilot on 20 AV loads, then $60 per handoff. Sign a cargo insurer as design partner to co-develop the claims-evidence package.

title: Disposable Ocean Drifters Reporting Through Orbit
one_liner: $10-30 drifting sensors dropped from passing ships that report through Bluetooth-to-satellite links, building a dense ocean nowcast.
customer: Weather-routing companies, offshore wind and energy operators, hurricane-season shipping and fishing fleets, insurers and coast guards.
problem: Ocean observation is sparse and expensive, because standard buoys cost thousands of dollars each, and some public observing networks have reportedly lost capacity. Routing and offshore-operations customers pay for better current, wave and sea-surface data.
solution: A disposable floating sensor (GPS, temperature, basic wave motion) that uses a standard Bluetooth chip and a Bluetooth-to-satellite network for uplink. Recruit ships of opportunity (research vessels, yacht races, cargo lines) to deploy hundreds. Sell a nowcast layer and event-specific coverage such as hurricane drifts.
why_now: Hubble Network (6 satellites, $200M Series C) shows ordinary Bluetooth chips can reach orbit, and its next generation improves link margins. Sensors and uplink are now cheap enough for disposable use.
revenue_model: Data subscriptions $20-100k per year per routing or offshore customer. Event campaigns of $50-200k. Sensor kits sold at cost to research and racing fleets.
non_obvious_insight: Cheap satellite uplink flips ocean sensing from a few expensive fixed buoys to millions of throwaway ones, and ships already crossing the ocean provide free deployment.
first_30_days: Build 50 prototype drifters and test the link at sea on a partner yacht or research cruise. Sign two weather-routing or offshore wind customers for paid pilots before the next hurricane season.

title: Independent Leakage Audits for Age Verification
one_liner: A red-team lab that measures how easily under-16s slip past each platform's age check (VPN, borrowed ID, face tricks) and sells defensible evidence to platforms, counsel and insurers.
customer: Mid-size social, gaming and video platforms operating in Australia, the UK, Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia and US ban states. Also their outside counsel and, later, regulators.
problem: Insiders treat age assurance as a vendor-selection problem. Regulators judge whether 'reasonable steps' were taken. Australia is investigating five major platforms (fines up to A$49.5M) and proposed in June 2026 to double fines to about A$99M and reach app stores and age-assurance providers. By February 2026 many children had already bypassed the ban. Vendors self-report accuracy but nobody independently measures real-world leakage at the 14-17 border.
solution: A standard test harness of about 20 evasion scenarios (VPN region switch, parent's ID, older-sibling account, face-estimation edge cases, re-registration). It runs with consented adult testers and synthetic profiles, never with minors. Outputs are a quarterly public 'Leakage Index' plus confidential 'reasonable-steps evidence packs' and a continuous monitoring subscription.
why_now: Bans went live between December 2025 and June 2026 and enforcement is starting. The proposed extension of liability to age-assurance providers means everyone in the chain wants third-party evidence. The reported IDScan breach and Persona complaints (both from the brief, one flagged shaky) push platforms to question their vendors.
revenue_model: Confidential audits at $15-60k each. Monitoring subscription at $3-10k a month. Later, licensing the test protocol to regulators and insurers.
non_obvious_insight: This is an assurance market like SOC 2, not a technology market. The buyer wants a defensible paper trail, and it must be independent of the vendors it grades, so the lab should be paid by the platforms rather than the vendors.
first_30_days: Write the 20-scenario protocol with a regulatory lawyer. Run it on 5 public age gates in Australia using adult test accounts, keeping to what counsel clears. Publish a free 'Leakage Index' teaser. Cold-email trust-and-safety leads and regulatory counsel at 40 mid-size platforms with their own results.

title: Kitchen Circuit Retrofit for India's Induction Switch
one_liner: Induction demand is real but low-income wiring cannot handle it, so sell the safe electrical retrofit and finance it.
customer: Lower-income urban households and resident welfare associations, reached through local electricians and hardware shops; discoms and state schemes can co-fund.
problem: After the LPG shortage, induction cooktop demand jumped 20-25x, the government is handing out 500k stoves, and the shift could add up to 27 GW. The Hindu reports low-income uptake is sluggish because of old wiring, overloaded meters and no financing.
solution: A pre-certified plug-and-play kit: dedicated 16A circuit, MCB/RCCB, heavy-duty socket and load-limiting smart plug, installed in two hours and paid in 12 EMIs. The wedge is 500 homes in one city through about 30 electricians.
why_now: The Hormuz energy shock created panic demand in March 2026, and the grid and household wiring are the binding constraint.
revenue_model: Rs 2,500-4,000 per kit and install at about 30% margin, plus an EMI spread and programme fees from discoms.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone counts stoves sold. The bottleneck is the last 15 metres of copper, and the first fire wave will turn certified retrofits into a regulated must-buy.
first_30_days: Design the kit with a licensed electrical engineer and pre-sell it through 20 electricians and one housing association.

title: Dark-Core Muscle Clinics in Converting Offices
one_liner: A plug-in metabolic and muscle clinic sized for the windowless middle of deep office floor plates that developers cannot turn into apartments, so dead space earns rent and GLP-1 users get an in-building place to keep their muscle.
customer: Office-to-residential developers and their lenders with deep-floorplate buildings (they gain a rent line on unusable area). Demand side: GLP-1 users who live or work in the building, plus employers that dropped GLP-1 coverage (employer coverage fell from 72% to 60% in 2026) and want a capped-cost program.
problem: Conversions only pencil when every bedroom can have a window, so deep floor plates lose a large share of each floor to unrentable middle or need expensive light wells. Meanwhile only about a third of non-diabetic GLP-1 patients persist at 1 year, stoppers regain weight roughly 4x faster than behavioral losers, and muscle loss is unmanaged. Nobody is paid to run a supervised strength-and-nutrition protocol close to where patients live and work.
solution: A standardized 3,000-6,000 sf module: body-composition scan, 6-8 supervised strength stations, dietitian rooms, lab draw, telehealth booths and pill-pickup lockers, run by a prescriber-agnostic clinical group so members can bring a Wegovy or Foundayo script from anywhere. Ambulatory clinics are Group B occupancy like offices, so no change of use is needed. Developers get a 'core-fill' master lease (low $/sf plus a slice of membership revenue) that improves conversion math and gives lenders a credit-tested income line. Members pay about $99/mo. Employers pay a capped per-employee fee.
why_now: The Wegovy pill (Jan 2026) and Lilly's Foundayo (Apr 2026) at about $149/mo turned GLP-1s into a mass cash-pay product, so millions of stop-and-restart cycles are coming. Employers are dropping coverage. Office vacancy is 17.8% with $289B of office loans maturing by 2028 and CMBS delinquency at 13.2%, so owners will trade rent for feasibility. Neko Health's $700M raise for a NYC launch shows urban demand for preventive scanning, yet nobody runs the muscle-and-adherence loop after the scan.
revenue_model: Memberships at $79-149/mo; per-member fees from employers and Medicare Advantage plans; body-comp and lab add-ons; a low-rent master lease with revenue share to the landlord.
non_obvious_insight: The thing that kills conversions (no daylight) is the one thing a clinic does not need. Because clinics share office occupancy class, the space is code-legal without a change of use. A clinic inside the building where hundreds of residents and lunch-hour office workers already are may be the highest-adherence location possible for a persistence problem.
first_30_days: Lease one vacant interior suite in a half-empty Class B office at near-zero rent with landlord-funded build-out. Open a 10-week 'GLP-1 muscle lab' with one exercise physiologist, a $10-15K body-composition scanner and a contracted dietitian. Sell 40-60 memberships to workers in the building and 2-3 local employers that dropped coverage. Take the adherence data to conversion developers with deep-plate buildings and sign 1-2 letters of intent.

title: Narrow Networks and Reference Pricing for Pet Insurers
one_liner: Pet insurers reimburse whatever clinics invoice while losing about 10 points a year to price/mix inflation; build the pet-insurance 'PPO' from affordable-care clinics whose invoices run about 44% lower.
customer: Mid-size pet insurers and MGAs (payers), affordable-care and team-based independent clinics (network), and insured owners steered by a lower deductible or higher reimbursement in-network.
problem: 2025 premiums grew about 19.7% against 9% growth in insured animals, and insurers do not contract with clinics, so they have no lever on price. Owners face renewal shock. Corporate chains (Mars about 2,100 clinics; GoodVets going from 75 to 116) are bound to margin targets and are unlikely to cut price.
solution: Contract a metro-by-metro network of independent affordable-care clinics with agreed fee schedules, standardized service coding and direct pay. The insurer offers an in-network tier (for example, 90% reimbursement with no deductible on routine lines). We provide claims routing, spectrum-of-care quality guardrails, and network-savings reporting. Start with one metro.
why_now: The premium/enrollment gap is now visible in trade press, roll-ups are accelerating, and the affordable-care model is documented at $130 vs $233 average invoices. Model-law adoption is pushing insurers toward transparency and cost containment.
revenue_model: Shared savings (20-30% of verified savings vs a market baseline) or 3-5% administration fee on network claims. Clinics pay nothing.
non_obvious_insight: 'Reimburse at any vet' is sold as a feature, but in human health the equivalent indemnity design gave way to networks once cost trend outran wages. Steering is the only demand-side lever pet insurance has not pulled, and the low-priced independent tier is spare capacity waiting for volume.
first_30_days: Identify 15-20 team-based or low-cost independents in one metro. Get an NDA with one small insurer or MGA and pull 200 claims. Reprice them against the network fee schedule to show projected savings (target 15% or more). Propose a 6-month shared-savings pilot on an existing product tier.

title: GitHub Outage Hot-Standby Forge
one_liner: A managed Forgejo standby that continuously mirrors repos, PRs, issues and Actions workflows, runs monthly failover drills, and lets a team ship a hotfix in minutes when GitHub is down, so nobody has to migrate off GitHub.
customer: Engineering teams of 5-200 with on-call rotations and release SLAs (B2B SaaS, fintech, agencies), plus EU firms who want a sovereignty story. They pay $8-12 per developer per month, or $99/month flat for teams of 10 or fewer.
problem: Ask HN 'Alternatives to GitHub' hit 649 points and 437 comments on 17 August 2026: 'Github has been down consistently over the last few months'; one team 'had to delay a release due to Github being down'; another said GitHub exceeded in two months a downtime budget its self-hosted GitLab had used only 1.5 days of in six years. The blockers cited for actually leaving are GitHub Actions lock-in, the PR workflow and ecosystem, not git hosting. Teams that do leave need 1-3 people to run a forge.
solution: A GitHub App that syncs code, tags, releases, and (read-write for a defined subset) PRs and issues into a managed per-customer Forgejo instance. A workflow portability linter tells the customer which of their Actions workflows will fail on Forgejo runners and proposes patches. Secrets are synced opt-in and encrypted. A break-glass switch redirects the deploy pipeline to standby runners (Forgejo v15 runs Kubernetes-native ephemeral runners). Monthly automated fire drills execute the customer's real deploy against staging in standby and produce a dated 'last successful failover' badge and status page for customers' security questionnaires.
why_now: GitHub instability through 2026, Forgejo Actions now described by users as 'near 1:1' with GitHub Actions, Forgejo v15's runner improvements (August 2026), and an AI-coding PR and CI volume surge that makes every hour of downtime costlier.
revenue_model: Per-developer subscription ($8-12/dev/month), $99/month flat for small teams, plus runner-minute overage and an enterprise tier with EU-only hosting and SSO.
non_obvious_insight: The 437-comment thread is framed as 'leave GitHub', but the stated blockers mean most teams will not, so the product that gets paid for is insurance rather than migration. Insurance is priced on drill evidence: a dated failover-drill badge is what a CTO can show a customer's procurement team. The open-source workflow linter is the wedge. Evidence: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49331033 (outage complaints, Actions as primary blocker, 'delay a release'); Forgejo Actions compatibility claims and DIY setups costing $60/month for a Kubernetes cluster https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48473170 and https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49360197.
first_30_days: Release a free open-source CLI that scores a repo's Actions workflows for Forgejo portability and post it in the GitHub-alternatives thread. Stand up a multi-tenant Forgejo with mirror sync in a few weeks using existing Forgejo, its runner and a sync service. Offer a $99/month founding-customer plan to the commenters who delayed releases and to 20 SaaS teams with uptime SLAs. Run the first joint failover drill with each design partner in week 4.

title: Dumpster-Drop Leads for the Next Trade
one_liner: A white-label booking flow for independent roll-off dumpster companies that sells the homeowner's renovation start as an exclusive, unshared lead to the next trade in sequence.
customer: Local electricians, plumbers, drywall and paint, flooring and roofing shops pay per exclusive lead. Independent roll-off haulers (10-40 trucks) get revenue share and better booking software.
problem: 73% of homeowners have unstarted projects, 78% of them have no quotes, and the barriers are 'too busy' (21%), trust (21%) and no response (14%). Homeowner-plus-pro jobs rose from 27% to 46% while DIY-only fell from 50% to 39%. Angi charges $15-85 per lead and resells each to many bidders, and about 48% of home-service calls never reach a person.
solution: When a homeowner books a 10-30 yard bin, a two-question flow captures project type, timing, budget and lead-sharing consent. The hauler recommends one pre-vetted pro for the next step (electrical rough-in after demo, flooring after tear-out), with no bidding. The pro pays $50-120 only for an accepted lead. Drivers confirm project stage at swap-outs.
why_now: The DIY-plus-pro shift makes the demo-and-haul step the natural first purchase. Distrust of shared-lead marketplaces is high, and cheap AI text and voice booking lets small haulers add a lead flow without staff. Median home age is 44 years and remodeling spend hit a record $524B.
revenue_model: Per exclusive lead, about 40% shared with the hauler; SaaS for haulers at $99-299/mo; a recycled-C&D upsell.
non_obvious_insight: The dumpster is the earliest hard commitment in a remodel: money is spent and demo starts within days. The hauler is a locally trusted, neutral party that sees demand before any contractor quotes it. Its leads are exclusive, which is the opposite of Angi's economics.
first_30_days: Sign 3 independent haulers in one metro. Add consent and project questions to their web and phone booking. Recruit 6 pros (one per trade) at about $60 per exclusive lead. Measure booking-to-job conversion for a month and tune the trade sequence before adding metros.

title: Contingency Appeals for Denied Pet Insurance Claims
one_liner: Insurers rely on paperwork friction to keep denials uncontested; LLMs that assemble records and policy language make appeals cheap enough to work for a success fee.
customer: Pet owners with denied or reduced claims of roughly $1,500-$15,000 (pre-existing, bilateral, hereditary or 'curable' exclusion disputes), reached through owner communities and vet front desks.
problem: Premiums rose about 19.7% in 2025 while insured animals grew 9%, so owners are angry and paying more for coverage that may not pay. An appeal requires pulling every prior clinic's records, reading policy definitions and getting a vet statement. Most owners give up.
solution: Owner uploads the denial letter and policy. We automate records requests to past clinics, read records against the policy's definitions and the state's pet-insurance rules, draft the appeal with a contracted DVM's signed medical statement, file it, and escalate to the state insurance department if needed. Fee is 15-25% of recovered dollars, nothing upfront.
why_now: As of early 2026, 28 states had adopted or introduced versions of the NAIC Pet Insurance Model Act, which creates disclosure and pre-existing-condition hooks and formal complaint routes. LLMs can now read messy multi-clinic records cheaply. Premium hikes are driving search intent and anger.
revenue_model: Contingency fee of 15-25% of recovered claims. Second product: anonymized denial-pattern intelligence sold to regulators, clinics and insurers who want fewer disputes.
non_obvious_insight: Denial rates are sustained by the cost of contesting, not by the merits. That cost was human labor. Once evidence assembly is near-free, the spread between 'denied' and 'overturned when documented' becomes a business, and it produces the best dataset on how insurers actually deny.
first_30_days: Post 'no win, no fee appeals' in pet-owner communities and take 30 cases. Contract one vet to sign statements at $75-150 each. Track overturn rate; kill criterion is under 20%. Check state public-adjuster and unauthorized-practice rules before charging a contingency fee.

title: After-Death Home Reset for Hospice Families
one_liner: A two-person crew that returns the house to normal within 48 hours of a home hospice death: bed out, meds destroyed, room restored, memory box packed.
customer: Hospice agencies pay per home death, as a family-experience and bereavement differentiator. A second stream is families paying a premium, and funeral homes reselling it as an add-on.
problem: After a home death the hospital bed, oxygen concentrator and commode often sit in the living room for days. The DME vendor schedules pickup on its own clock. The leftover morphine, lorazepam and haloperidol 'comfort kit' sits in the fridge or cabinet. Nurses are supposed to see to disposal, but the home visit is often skipped or rushed, and families quietly keep or mis-dispose of them. The dead person's glasses, dentures and hearing aids end up in a drawer. The family remembers the empty bed in the middle of the room for the rest of their lives. The CAHPS Hospice family survey arrives months later and those last impressions color the answers.
solution: A chaplain-designed protocol delivered by two trained, background-checked staff in a branded van. On admission, the hospice photographs the room so the crew can restore the original furniture layout. Within 24 to 48 hours of death the crew coordinates or performs bed and equipment removal, destroys leftover controlled drugs with deactivation pouches and a witnessed log the hospice can put in the chart, and launders linens. They pack a memory box (glasses, jewelry, a worn shirt, the last handwritten note). They restore the room, open the windows, and offer a two-minute optional blessing or silence. A hand-off card tells the family what happens at 2 weeks and 6 weeks.
why_now: Hospice is consolidating, with private equity and large chains competing on public CAHPS-based quality scores that drive referrals. Regulators and communities are paying more attention to opioid diversion. Hospice per-diem margins are squeezed and the DME vendors they use are getting slower and cheaper. Home is where most hospice deaths occur. Also, nurses are stretched thin, so the care they used to give informally in that first day is disappearing, and nobody owns it.
revenue_model: Hospice pays $250 to $400 per home death on a per-case contract, with volume tiers. Families or funeral homes pay $450 to $600 for a premium version with a full room refresh and donation pickup for clothing and mobility aids. A hospice with roughly 100 patients on service has on the order of 25 to 35 deaths a month, around half at home, so three hospices support a small crew. Sponsorship from a nonprofit hospice foundation can cover indigent families.
non_obvious_insight: Outsiders think the crisis is the moment of death. Insiders know the emotional injury persists in the physical room and in the loose ends nobody owns: the bed, the drugs, the dentures. The hospice would love to solve it but cannot bill for it and the nurse has already left. Whoever owns hours 6 through 48 after death, when the funeral home has taken the body and all clinical staff have gone, owns the family's memory of the hospice.
first_30_days: Sign one small nonprofit hospice as a design partner. Write the checklist with the chaplain, the DON and a pharmacist for the controlled-drug disposal log. Buy a used van, get general liability coverage, and hire two people with home-health-aide or hospitality backgrounds. Do the first 5 to 8 resets free in exchange for family feedback. Charge from case 9, and ask the hospice's quality director to compare family feedback scores with and without the reset.

title: Scam-Spell Breakers: Human Callbacks for Seniors
one_liner: A human 'callback' service in which ex-call-center agents are trained to talk older customers out of scams, sold to credit unions and community banks as a per-member protection benefit.
customer: Community banks and credit unions (5k-200k members), also Medicare Advantage plans, and families via a $19/month consumer plan. Banks pay about $0.40-1.00 per member per month or $75-150 per intervention.
problem: The FBI's 2025 IC3 report (April 2026) shows Americans over 60 lost $7.75B, up 59%, with more than 3,100 senior complaints citing AI. Detection systems flag transactions, but victims coached by scammers ignore warnings and lie to tellers. Frontline staff lack the time and training for the delicate conversation that breaks the scammer's hold without shaming the victim.
solution: When a bank's system flags a large or unusual transfer by a senior, the transaction is held and a trained spell-breaker calls within minutes. They use scam-specific playbooks (romance, crypto investment, tech support) based on motivational interviewing, guide the customer to verify independently with a trusted family member, and document the outcome. They also enroll a trusted-contact circle and run monthly check-ins. Reports show dollars saved per dollar of fees.
why_now: Elder-fraud losses and AI-voice-clone scams are rising sharply, while banks face regulatory and reputational pressure to show duty of care. Call-center layoffs create a large pool of people with exactly this skill set.
revenue_model: Per-member-per-month bank contracts, per-intervention fees, a consumer family plan, and outcome-based bonuses tied to verified saves.
non_obvious_insight: Scam interception is a rapport problem, not a detection problem, and the best call-center agents' skills of de-escalation, listening, and warm scripts transfer directly. The ROI is unusually crisp for a services business: dollars saved versus fees, which gives an easy pitch to a CFO or board.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 ex-agents and train them with retired fraud investigators and a social worker. Approach 3 credit unions through state leagues and offer a 90-day, success-priced pilot using the credit union's existing fraud alerts and a purely phone-based workflow. Aim for one paid pilot within 60-90 days.

title: Agentic Crypto Trace-and-Freeze Desk for Police
one_liner: An AI forensic analyst that traces a victim's stolen crypto across chains in minutes and drafts freeze requests, sold to local police who receive these reports but cannot trace.
customer: Police and sheriff's fraud and elder-crimes units, state AG consumer units, victim-service nonprofits and credit unions.
problem: Crypto-related complaints hit 181,565 and $11.4B in 2025, and victims report to local police who lack $20K+ blockchain forensics tools and training. Funds hop through swaps, bridges and exchange deposit addresses, and freeze windows are measured in hours.
solution: An officer or victim enters a transaction hash and an agent traces flows across major chains and bridges, clusters to exchange deposit addresses using open labels, and produces a freeze packet (evidence PDF and correctly formatted requests to exchange law-enforcement portals and stablecoin issuers). The officer approves, and recovery outcomes are tracked.
why_now: Tool-using agents can now run chain-analysis workflows and draft legal requests. Stablecoin issuers are cooperating on freezes at scale, and scam flows concentrate in a few tokens and exchanges.
revenue_model: $3-10K per agency per year, or about $150 per case, with elder-justice grant funding.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck in crypto recovery is procedural delivery, not analytics: which desk accepts what format, and how fast. An agent that sends the right request in minutes matters more than another dashboard.
first_30_days: Build tracing for USDT on Tron and Ethereum plus Bitcoin to the top 10 exchanges. Offer free traces to 10 sheriff's offices, track freezes, publish outcomes, and start $250 per month pilots with elder-justice grant funding lined up.

title: Fuel Surcharge Autopilot for Route-Based Services
one_liner: An add-on for field-service software that adds a transparent, index-linked, capped and self-expiring fuel line to invoices, and explains it to customers.
customer: Small route-based service businesses with 3-50 trucks: lawn and landscape, pest control, pool service, septic and portable toilets, HVAC and plumbing, mobile detailing and small waste haulers. They pay a monthly fee.
problem: Diesel is $6.53/gal, up $2.78 from a year ago, and gasoline is $4.48. Large firms absorb it. Cintas says 'we do not pass through any fuel surcharges', and Darden says sustained $6+ diesel would add 10-15 bps of cost. Small operators eat the increase or raise base prices and lose customers, because a surcharge added ad hoc looks like a scam.
solution: A plug-in for Jobber, Housecall Pro, Service Autopilot, Workiz and QuickBooks. The owner sets a base fuel price and a mileage-per-job model, and the plug-in computes a per-visit surcharge from the weekly EIA regional diesel or gasoline index. It adds a labelled invoice line with a cap, sends a one-time customer notice using tested wording, auto-reduces the charge when prices fall, and shows the owner recovered margin. The customer sees a public methodology page.
why_now: The Iran-conflict fuel shock has been running since spring, with diesel up 74% year over year, and it now appears in every large company's guidance (Darden, KB Home, General Mills, AutoZone, Stitch Fix). Small service businesses have had months of margin erosion and lack the pricing staff that large companies use.
revenue_model: $19-$49/month per business, or a 3-5% share of surcharge dollars collected. Add an annual 'fuel and route cost' benchmark report for FSM platforms as a lead generator.
non_obvious_insight: Fuel is a trust problem, not a math problem. The EIA shows diesel at $6.529/gal on Sept 21, 2026, up $2.780 year over year, with gasoline at $4.478 (https://www.eia.gov/petroleum/gasdiesel/). Cintas's CEO says 'it's a volatile situation with the price at the pump. We do not pass through any fuel surcharges' (https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/24/cintas-ctas-q1-2027-earnings-call-transcript/). Darden's CFO puts the risk from sustained elevated diesel at 10-15 bps of sales and says its delivery fees sit in fixed-price contracts (https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/24/darden-dri-q1-2027-earnings-call-transcript/). H.B. Fuller says small and mid-sized customers' order patterns swing on oil headlines (https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/24/fuller-ful-q3-2026-earnings-call-transcript/). Small operators cannot afford the customer backlash that large companies can, so a public formula, a cap and an automatic expiry are the product. Field-service platforms have not built this. The risk is that Jobber or ServiceTitan ship it natively, so the plan is to sell to the operator through a marketplace listing first and move quickly.
first_30_days: Build a minimal version as a Jobber integration or a Zapier plus Google Sheets tool driven by the EIA diesel API. Post in landscaping, pest and pool operator communities (Facebook groups, r/lawncare, LawnSite, PCT forums) offering a free tool and template customer letter. Get 20 operators to run it for one billing cycle, measure surcharge acceptance and cancellations, then start charging $29/month. Apply to the Jobber and Housecall Pro app marketplaces in parallel.

title: Hospice for Dying Congregations
one_liner: A managed 'final season' service for congregations that are closing, covering the closing liturgy, an oral-history archive, member placement and a community-first sale of the building.
customer: Denominational regional bodies (dioceses, presbyteries, conferences) and individual congregations with fewer than 50 members deciding to close, and community land trusts and developers who want to reuse their buildings.
problem: Lifeway reported 4,000 Protestant closures against 3,800 openings in 2024, and shrinking, aging congregations keep sliding toward closure. The process is legally messy (deeds, endowments, cemeteries, records, sacred objects) and emotionally painful, and it usually ends in a rushed sale to whoever pays most, with members scattering and often falling out of community altogether.
solution: A 6-12 month managed process: a closing service designed with celebrants, a professional oral-history and photo archive digitised for the community, guided placement of members into neighbouring congregations or community groups, and stewardship of stained glass, organs and memorial gifts. We run a request-for-proposals that favours reuse (housing, community centres) under a mission covenant.
why_now: Post-COVID closures never fully rebounded, clergy are aging, and denominations are sitting on stranded property. California's 2023 law allowing affordable housing on faith-owned land, and the copycat 'YIGBY' bills in other states, make community reuse financially viable.
revenue_model: A fixed fee of roughly $15-40k per congregation paid by the denomination or from sale proceeds, plus a 1-3% success fee on community-reuse sales. Optional licensing of archives to historians, genealogists and local libraries.
non_obvious_insight: Dying congregations do not lack real-estate brokers; they lack a good funeral and a dignified narrative. That is the real barrier to a good sale, because grieving members block anything that feels like betrayal. Whoever holds the funeral earns the trust to shape the outcome toward community use, so you sell a good death and earn the property fee as a consequence.
first_30_days: List 20 congregations flagged for closure in a single denomination region. Offer three subsidised 'Last Sunday' packages at about $5k each, and use the outcomes to pitch the regional executive on a standing contract.

title: Circle Cue: Name Whispers for Early Dementia
one_liner: Consent-only Bluetooth badges let earbuds whisper who a person is and one line of context to someone with mild cognitive impairment, with no cameras and no face recognition.
customer: Families of people with mild cognitive impairment or early Alzheimer's ($149 kit plus $15 a month), memory cafes, senior centers and faith groups, and later Medicare Advantage plans and dementia-care programs.
problem: People in early dementia often withdraw because forgetting names is humiliating, and caregivers watch the social world shrink. Face-recognition glasses are legally and ethically fraught (biometric-privacy laws), and dementia technology focuses on safety tracking rather than social participation.
solution: Circle members (family, neighbors, club regulars) opt in by wearing small Bluetooth badges with rotating IDs. The user's phone detects nearby IDs and whispers, for example, 'Tom Reyes, your neighbor; knee surgery last month' from a one-line card written by the circle and managed by the caregiver. It works offline and cards expire to avoid stale information.
why_now: Cheap BLE, on-device speech and summarization, and LE Audio earbuds make this cheap to build. FDA-cleared Alzheimer's blood tests (2025) and anti-amyloid drugs are pushing diagnosis earlier, creating a fast-growing population that is cognitively capable and socially at risk for years.
revenue_model: Hardware kit, monthly subscription, and B2B circle licenses for memory cafes and senior centers. Later: plan-funded coverage.
non_obvious_insight: The privacy-safe alternative to face recognition is consent by badge: a small, fully opt-in social graph of 10-30 people that covers most of what the person meets each week. Consent is the feature, and it turns surveillance tech into hospitality.
first_30_days: Partner with three memory cafes. Make 30 badges (about $4 each) and a prototype app. Trial with five families free, measure outings per week before and after, then sell $149 kits.

title: Pickleball Court Noise Pre-Clearance Reports
one_liner: Standardized acoustic siting reports and low-cost monitoring loggers that let HOAs, senior communities and parks approve or defend pickleball courts before neighbors sue.
customer: HOA and condo boards, management companies, 55+ and retirement communities adding courts, city parks departments, and hotels, gyms and churches that want courts. They pay $1,200-$3,500 per site, plus a monthly logger rental. Complainant attorneys are a secondary buyer.
problem: Pickleball's popping sound is a legal flashpoint. In February 2026 two homeowners in Parkside at Boca Trail (203 homes) sued to shut two courts. Testing found up to 73 dB against a 55 dB city nuisance threshold, about 900 pops per hour, and nearest homes only 67-72 feet away versus the 300-500 feet often recommended. The homeowners have spent over $50,000 in legal fees, and the HOA paid $3,800 for an acoustic study. A 2023 survey found only 30% of residents wanted the courts unchanged and 28% wanted them closed. Boards cannot get neutral, standard evidence.
solution: A 'Court Siting Certificate'. It uses a calibrated Class 2 sound-level meter and a fixed protocol (LAmax, LAeq and 1-4 kHz pop-band readings at property lines and the nearest homes), then models the results against that municipality's ordinance. We keep a database of local noise ordinances and hours rules for the fastest-growing pickleball markets. The report ranks mitigation options by dB reduction per dollar: USA Pickleball's Quiet Category paddles and balls, acoustic fencing, hours limits and court orientation. A signed, board-meeting-ready PDF follows. Boards can also rent solar-powered sound loggers at $99/month to produce a continuous dB record for disputes.
why_now: Pickleball searches are about 8.4M (+42%). Glimpse reports retirement homes 'rushing to add the sport' and $10 CPCs. Lawsuits are arriving in 2026, the Boca Raton case being the first of its kind in Palm Beach County, and boards are converting tennis courts (this HOA did so in 2021). Every new court adds exposure.
revenue_model: $1,200-$3,500 per pre-clearance report or dispute audit, $99/month logger rental with monthly compliance reports, and referral fees from acoustic-fence installers and quiet-equipment retailers. Later: annual retainers with HOA management companies covering 50+ communities.
non_obvious_insight: Boards are not really buying noise reduction. They are buying neutral evidence and a defensible process before the fight starts. The Boca Raton case shows the asymmetry: a $3,800 study against $50,000+ in resident legal fees, with a split community (https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/pickleball-noise-sparks-lawsuit-tony-123055657.html). Glimpse's trend data flags pickleball demand among seniors and retirement homes (https://meetglimpse.com/trends/). The popular advice articles offer 'acoustic fencing, sound barriers, landscaping, buffer zones' but no costs, standards or benchmarks (https://spinwavepickleball.com/a/blog/pickleball-noise). A published, comparable measurement standard becomes the reference document that lawyers, city staff and boards all cite.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: buy two Class 2 meters and write the measurement protocol and report template, and compile ordinances for Florida, Arizona, Texas, the Carolinas and California metros. Days 8-20: cold-email 200 HOA management firms and community managers with a $750 pilot audit offer, and publish a 'pickleball noise ordinance by city' page for SEO. Days 21-30: complete 5 audits, get one board to publicly cite the report, and sign an installer referral partnership.

title: Work-Share Desk: Kurzarbeit for American Employers
one_liner: Administer state short-time compensation for mid-size employers so they can cut hours 20-40% instead of laying off skilled staff, with workers drawing pro-rated unemployment benefits.
customer: Employers with 50-800 employees (manufacturers, distributors, engineering firms, PEO-served businesses) in states with work-share programs, buying through the CFO, HR head or PEO.
problem: Roughly 33 states have short-time compensation programs, yet take-up is tiny because employers do not know they exist and the paperwork (plan applications, weekly certifications, state-specific rules, payroll integration) is painful. Layoffs then destroy trained staff who cost one to two times salary to replace when demand returns.
solution: A layoff-versus-work-share calculator for CFOs, plus a done-for-you service. It checks eligibility, prepares the state plan, connects payroll (Gusto, ADP, Rippling) to generate weekly certification data, provides employee communication scripts and tracks the effect on the employer's unemployment account. Expand state by state and through PEOs and manufacturers' associations.
why_now: The oil shock (crude above $100, diesel near $6) and the September 2026 Fed hike, the first since 2023, are cooling consumers. Unemployment is still low at about 4.1%, so executives want to keep hard-to-replace workers and are wary of repeating the 2022-2023 layoff-then-rehire cycle.
revenue_model: $1,500-3,000 setup fee plus $10-15 per participating employee per week, or 15% of verified savings versus layoff and rehire. PEO channel revenue share.
non_obvious_insight: The program exists but nobody built the admin layer because the payoff only arrives in downturns. This is a business that sells the same product every recession and can build its state-rule database and PEO channel during the quiet years. Retention value is high precisely because the labor market is still tight.
first_30_days: Pick two manufacturing-heavy states with simple program rules (for example Ohio, Michigan or Pennsylvania). Publish a free layoff-versus-work-share calculator. Pitch 30 manufacturers via associations and PEOs and sign 5-10 at a $1,500 flat setup fee, doing the paperwork by hand at first.

title: Blank-First Microplastics: Clean Kits and Data Forensics
one_liner: Sell certified low-shed sampling kits, blank/spike proficiency samples, and legacy-data re-analysis to microplastics labs whose glove-contaminated numbers are now in doubt.
customer: Environmental testing labs pursuing state microplastics accreditation, public water utilities that must test and report, university microplastics groups, and beverage/bottled-water QA labs. Litigation and NGO teams that need defensible numbers are a secondary buyer.
problem: Routine nitrile and latex gloves shed stearate particles that read as microplastics, adding about 2,000 false-positive signals per mm² in University of Michigan tests. Labs are 'searching for the needle in the haystack' and are unsure how much of their existing data is contaminated. Labs cannot reliably tell real microplastics from consumable-derived artifacts.
solution: 1) 'Blank-first' kits with characterized cleanroom gloves, pre-cleaned filters, slides and foil, plus lot-level FTIR/Raman shed certificates. 2) Blind spiked reference samples for inter-lab proficiency checks. 3) A data-forensics service that re-screens a lab's archived spectra and micrographs for stearate signatures, using the published discrimination approach. 4) A public 'shed scoreboard' of glove and consumable brands to build trust and inbound leads.
why_now: The Michigan glove-artifact paper appeared in RSC Analytical Methods in 2026, and it says affected datasets can potentially be recovered. California's drinking-water microplastics program (SB 1422) has adopted IR and Raman methods and plans four years of testing and reporting. Its 22-lab intercomparison flagged accuracy and precision as needing improvement, so lab demand for defensible negatives is rising just as the artifact becomes public.
revenue_model: Consumable kits at roughly $300-1,000 per kit with recurring lot replenishment. Proficiency-sample subscriptions at roughly $2-5k per lab per year. Fixed-price legacy-data re-analysis packages at roughly $5-25k, and certification-lot fees.
non_obvious_insight: In a measurement crisis the money is in negative controls, not in a better detector. The demand evidence is the University of Michigan finding of ~2,000 false positives/mm² from ordinary gloves and 'thousands of times higher than expected' counts (https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/03/260329222938.htm). California's inter-laboratory study also says methods need better accuracy and precision through training and refinement (https://www.waterboards.ca.gov/drinking_water/certlic/drinkingwater/microplastics.html). Every lab that ever wore nitrile gloves has a reason to buy reassurance, and the researchers themselves say old datasets can be salvaged, which creates a service market.
first_30_days: Buy about 10 glove brands, filters and slides, and run shed tests through a university core-facility FTIR or Raman instrument to produce a public shed scoreboard. Write to the paper's authors and about 30 accredited environmental labs and utility QA managers. Sell the first 10 pilot kits at cost-plus and offer 2-3 discounted forensic re-analyses in exchange for case studies.

title: Prize-Money Payout and Tax Rail for Tournaments
one_liner: Payout operations for tournament organizers and esports orgs: one-time player KYC and tax onboarding, treaty-aware withholding, sanctions screening, and multi-currency payment.
customer: Mid-tier tournament organizers (regional leagues, publisher-sanctioned circuits, fighting-game majors) and esports orgs receiving club-program stipends.
problem: Prize money exploded, with $75M at the 2026 Esports World Cup (moved to Paris) and a $20M club partner program across 40 orgs. Payments go to players in dozens of countries, including minors, with tax forms, withholding and sanctions checks, and organizers run it on spreadsheets and wire transfers.
solution: A payout platform with a portable 'player payout profile' (KYC and tax forms collected once), automated withholding by treaty, sanctions screening, escrowed prize pools released on verified results, and payment on local rails. Add visa and travel letter templates and year-end tax reporting.
why_now: Sovereign money inflated prize pools, and the Saudi-Olympic Esports Games partnership ending (2025-10-30) pushes more independent circuits. The compliance burden has grown with the money.
revenue_model: 1-2% of payout volume plus $3-8 per payee, and $500-3,000 per month SaaS for orgs.
non_obvious_insight: Prize pools stopped being a marketing line item and became a payments-and-tax operations problem. The onboarding data is portable across events, so each player carried through one event lowers the cost for the next organizer.
first_30_days: Interview 15 tournament organizers via start.gg and fighting-game communities. Run payouts manually for two events at 1.5% to learn the edge cases, and build the KYC and tax-form intake.

title: Audit-Grade Inventory Robots for Defense Property
one_liner: Drone and rover inventory counts that produce tamper-evident audit evidence, sold first to defense contractors who must physically inventory government-furnished property, then to Pentagon depots racing a clean-audit deadline.
customer: Property managers at small and mid-size defense contractors (machine shops, depot-level repair firms, integrators holding government property). Later, DoD depots and audit-readiness contractors that need count observation.
problem: DoD has never passed a full financial audit and has set a clean-opinion goal of about 2028 (verify), and inventory and materiel existence are among the biggest obstacles. Leaders admit they lack supply-chain data to support a '90-, 120-, 180-day fight'. Federal staff capacity is shrinking (OPM rating caps, contested reorganizations) and agencies keep buying capacity. Contractors holding government property (FAR 52.245-1) must keep records and do periodic physical inventories that DCMA property administrators review, and the work is manual and labor-heavy.
solution: Deploy indoor drones, rovers and wearable scanners to produce time-stamped, geotagged, hash-chained count evidence reconciled to property records. Output exception lists in the format auditors and property administrators expect. Use offline-first, air-gapped operation, since air-gap-native tooling (Defense Unicorns) cut authorization from 18 months to about 2 weeks. Begin in low-hazard bays and add ordnance-safe hardware later.
why_now: Warehouse inventory drones matured in commercial logistics but were never packaged for federal audit evidence. The Pentagon's comfort with small drones jumped through Drone Dominance, and audit-readiness spending is a live budget line. Federal staffing cuts push work to contractors.
revenue_model: Per verified location or per count event, priced below manual count crews, with annual recurring programs for contractors. Later, per-depot audit-evidence programs through subcontracts.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is not logistics but the CFO and audit-readiness office, which has a statutory deadline and money, while logistics chiefs have no robot budget. Selling robots as 'audit evidence' unlocks the funding. Contractor-held government property is a commercial beachhead with a private budget.
first_30_days: Recruit two defense contractors with large government-property holdings and one small audit or property-compliance firm. Do a free count at one facility to define the evidence format. Then price a paid annual inventory at each and pursue a small DLA or Army innovation solicitation.

title: Closed-Loop Solvents for the Generic GLP-1 Wave
one_liner: Solvent-recovery-as-a-service for peptide CDMOs and new generic semaglutide makers, because the pill era and the April 2026 patent expiries multiply peptide API output and its solvent waste.
customer: Generic GLP-1 manufacturers ramping in India (40+ launchers), Canada, Brazil, China and Turkey, plus peptide CDMOs and US peptide onshoring projects. The buyer is the plant's operations or EHS head, who is under margin pressure.
problem: Chemically synthesized and purified peptides are among the most solvent-hungry drugs (published process-mass-intensity estimates run around 10,000 kg of waste per kg of API, versus a few hundred for small molecules). Coupling and cleavage use DMF, NMP, DCM and TFA. RP-HPLC purification burns acetonitrile. DMF and NMP face tightening worker-exposure rules, and TFA is drawing PFAS scrutiny in Europe. Oral semaglutide needs about 25 mg a day versus 2.4 mg a week for the pen, roughly 70x more API per patient-week, so tonnage and waste balloon. Lilly's orforglipron is a small molecule and avoids this, so the burden lands on Novo's supply chain and the thin-margin generics.
solution: Containerized, GMP-adjacent recovery skids (fractional distillation, membrane polishing, carbon and ion-exchange for TFA capture) leased or run on a tolling basis. Recovered DMF and acetonitrile come back with a certificate of analysis for reuse in non-final steps, and a mass-balance ledger documents the reduced hazardous waste for regulators, auditors and customers. The first product is a paid batch-level solvent mass-balance audit, which leads to tolling.
why_now: Semaglutide patents expired across India, Canada, Brazil, China and Turkey around April 2026 and dozens of makers are scaling at once. The Wegovy pill launched Jan 5, 2026 and the pill format changes API volume by an order of magnitude or more. Solvent regulation is tightening. Acetonitrile has had repeated supply shocks.
revenue_model: Per-kg-recovered tolling fees, or a monthly skid lease plus a share of avoided virgin-solvent and incineration cost (customers typically keep 30-40% savings). Add-on fees for regulatory documentation.
non_obvious_insight: The GLP-1 story is told in doses, but its physical footprint is solvent mass. The second-tier generic makers who cannot afford incineration and cannot buy virgin acetonitrile at spot prices are the ones who will pay for recovery, not Novo or Lilly.
first_30_days: Offer five generic makers or CDMOs in Hyderabad, Ahmedabad and Ontario a free solvent mass-balance audit of one batch. Partner with an existing pharma-grade solvent tolling distiller so no capex is needed. Aim for one paid 5-10 tonne tolling pilot within 90 days and use the audit data to sell skid leases.

title: Rights-Cleared 1929-1963 Corpus for AI
one_liner: Join scanned mid-century books, magazines and newspapers to Copyright Office renewal records to produce provably public-domain text for AI training, with libraries paid a share and spared the scraper load.
customer: AI labs, foundation-model startups and fine-tuning shops that need litigation-proof training data, plus library and archive partners who supply scans (buyer is head of data or general counsel).
problem: Clean training data is now a legal necessity, but the best public-domain corpus (Harvard's Institutional Books 1.0, 983,004 volumes, 242B tokens) is largely pre-1929 text. For US works published 1929-1963, copyright lapsed unless renewed, yet renewals were rare (a 1961 Copyright Office study found fewer than 15% of registered copyrights renewed). The registration and renewal records exist but nobody has joined them to scanned text at scale. Meanwhile libraries are drowning in AI bots and have no sustainable way to offer their collections.
solution: Take scans that already exist (Internet Archive, partner libraries, HathiTrust-style holdings). Match each volume to Catalog of Copyright Entries registrations and renewals (Stanford renewal database for 1923-1949 books; Copyright Office online records for 1950+), and exclude foreign works restored under the URAA. Output a per-volume rights dossier with evidence links and a confidence score. Sell dataset snapshots with a signed provenance certificate (and insurance-backed warranty as revenue grows). Offer participating libraries a paid bulk-snapshot mirror (S3 or rsync) so AI buyers stop scraping their sites, with a revenue share.
why_now: The Authors Guild v. OpenAI/Microsoft unsealed briefs (2026-09-27) claim executives knew mass book piracy was illegal. Harvard and OpenAI/Microsoft-backed public-domain releases show buyers want clean data. Creative Commons (Aug 2026) says heritage institutions need standardized 'prosocial conditions' for AI access, and some (the National Library of the Netherlands, Trove) have closed access.
revenue_model: Dataset licenses ($25k-$250k per slice or annual refresh), provenance certificate fees, revenue share paid to libraries, bespoke rights-clearance projects for publishers reissuing out-of-print titles.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck for legal AI text isn't scanning, it's rights determination: a huge band of 1929-1963 US works is public domain because nobody filed a renewal, and it's invisible until someone does the record join at scale. Libraries currently do this by hand. Evidence: Institutional Books 1.0 covers 983,004 volumes and 242B tokens (https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08300). Wikipedia notes non-renewed pre-1964 works are public domain, the 1961 study, and the databases that hold the records (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copyright_renewal). GLAM-E Lab survey: 39 of 43 institutions (91%) saw traffic surges, 69% of those blamed AI training bots, 74% deployed countermeasures, and robots.txt was largely ignored (https://glamelab.org/products/are-ai-bots-knocking-cultural-heritage-offline/). Creative Commons Aug 2026 on institutions closing access (https://creativecommons.org/2026/08/19/open-heritage-in-the-age-of-artificial-intelligence/). Authors Guild briefs, HN 626 points (https://authorsguild.org/news/ag-v-openai-top-execs-knew-mass-book-piracy-was-illegal/).
first_30_days: Days 1-10: pick a narrow, high-value slice (for example 1950-1963 US trade, technical and hobby magazines where renewal was nearly nonexistent) and download the matching Internet Archive scans and renewal records. Days 10-25: run a first 5,000-volume join, have a copyright attorney sign off on the method and the URAA exclusions, and publish a free 500-volume sample with dossiers. Days 25-30: send the sample to 15 AI data buyers and licensed-data startups and to 5 mid-size libraries for a mirror pilot. Target one paid pilot in 90 days.
